title: Reading and fasting
hook: Megillah on reading Esther; Taanit on fasts and rain

segments.voice: Yesterday, seder and sukkah: a hut you can feel and four cups for every table. Your line was laws of joy. Did you give one good thing a little structure? Day one thousand seventy-five.

Say someone knows the whole book of Esther by heart. Every word, every name, every one of Haman's sons. On Purim night they stand up in front of the congregation, close their eyes, and recite it flawlessly. It's a beautiful performance. According to the Mishnah, it doesn't count. Next to that ruling sits another tractate, about fasting, which has its own surprise: a public fast where an elder stands up in the town square and tells the crowd that the fasting isn't the point. Two small tractates in the order of appointed times. Today: what they say about doing a thing for real.
screen: `ESTHER, BY HEART.` → `IT DOESN'T COUNT.` → `THE FASTING ISN'T THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Reading and fasting. First, Megillah, the tractate of the scroll. On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read from a scroll. The Mishnah sets the terms. Read it out of order, and you haven't fulfilled the duty. Read it from memory, and you haven't either. It has to be read from the written scroll, in order. But it also says that for people who speak another language, reading it in that language counts. So the rule is strict about the text and generous about the listener. The words on the page, in their order, reaching ears that understand them. Second, Taanit, the tractate of fasts. Much of it is about rain: when to begin praying for it in the autumn, and what a community does when the rains don't come. The answer is a series of public fasts. And here's the scene. On those fast days, says the Mishnah, the ark is carried out into the town square, ashes are put on it, and the eldest among them stands up to speak. He reminds the crowd of the people of Nineveh, who fasted in the book of Jonah. The verse doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." Works. Not the fast. The fast is the doorway, and the turning is the room. Third, the two belong together, and Esther shows why. In her story, before she goes to the king, she asks the Jews of Shushan to fast for her. The fast comes first, then the brave act. Reading and fasting: both are real only when something actually changes.
screen: `FROM THE SCROLL, IN ORDER.` · `IN A LANGUAGE YOU UNDERSTAND.` · `GOD SAW THEIR WORKS.` · `ESTHER FASTS, THEN ACTS.` · then, large: `READING AND FASTING.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: read one passage aloud. Choose something short. A few verses of Esther, a psalm, a paragraph from any book that matters to you. Read it from the page, not from memory, in order, out loud, slowly enough that you hear every word. Then put it down, and sit with your breath. What did you hear that you'd skipped before when you read it silently? Let one phrase stay with you. The bell holds the time.
Reading and fasting. Megillah, the scroll read from the page in order, and Taanit, the fasts that point beyond themselves to changed works. Today's word.
Your line: reading and fasting. Today, when you give something up, even a snack or a scroll through your phone, ask what work it's making room for. Day one thousand seventy-five.

howItsDone: On Purim, Jews gather to hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, often making noise at Haman's name; on public fast days, congregations add special prayers and the Torah reading for fasts.
